strengths: Novel research question bridging cognitive science and AI: investigates whether LLMs exhibit human-like biases toward semantic efficiency without explicit training
Sound theoretical framework: principled application of Information Bottleneck principle to understand semantic categorization
Creative methodology: IICLL paradigm cleverly adapts iterated language learning to test inductive biases beyond training data
Clear presentation: well-written paper with effective visualizations that communicate experimental design and results
Consistent empirical findings: robust convergence toward IB-efficiency across multiple metrics, generations, and initializations
Systematic comparison: tests multiple models (Gemini, Llama), input modalities (text, image), and provides good visualization of convergence trajectories
weaknesses: Severely limited scope: only one semantic domain (color) and two models; claims about "LLMs" in general are not supported; generalizability to other semantic categories unclear
Incomplete manuscript: missing citation '[?]' on page 2 indicates paper not fully prepared, raising quality concerns
Insufficient analysis of model differences: Llama shows systematically lower complexity than English, but explanations are speculative; differences undermine claims of universal IB bias
Unclear causal mechanism: paper shows convergence to IB-efficiency but doesn't prove this reflects an inductive bias versus other mechanisms like implicit pressure from next-token prediction training
Training data leakage inadequately addressed: Gemini's English alignment could reflect memorized patterns; pseudowords processed by models trained on billions of natural language examples
Missing methodological details: exact prompts, hyperparameters, and metric computation not specified; no ablations on sample size, categories, or initialization; significantly limits reproducibility
Weak baselines: no comparison with non-LLM systems or smaller models; unclear how much convergence is LLM-specific versus general to the IICLL process
Overstated claims: abstract and title use causal language ('reflect a learning bias') and broad generalization not warranted by single-domain evidence
Statistical analysis incomplete: no significance testing despite claims of robustness; source of randomness in 'random seeds' unclear
Generalization concerns: color naming is unique (continuous perceptual space, high cross-linguistic availability); findings may not extend to more abstract semantic categories

strengths: Novel and well-motivated research question connecting cognitive science and LLMs with clear relevance to understanding LLM alignment
Strong theoretical framework using Information Bottleneck principle with established grounding in cognitive science literature
Innovative IICLL methodology that cleverly adapts iterated language learning to probe implicit inductive biases beyond training data
Clear experimental design with two complementary studies (English color naming and IICLL convergence) that address different aspects of the research question
Comprehensive evaluation using multiple metrics (efficiency loss, IB-alignment, human-alignment) with clear visualizations of results
Interesting analysis of input modality effects (text vs. image) showing how representations influence model behavior
Well-written presentation with effective figures that communicate the theoretical framework and empirical results
weaknesses: Critical missing citations: Multiple '[? ]' placeholders in Section 3.2 appear to reference foundational prior work but are incomplete, suggesting insufficient manuscript preparation and hindering reproducibility
Severely limited generalizability: Evaluation restricted to single semantic domain (color naming); claims about LLMs evolving 'human-like semantic systems' are overgeneralized from narrow evidence
Very limited model coverage: Only two models tested; both are recent, high-capability models; most open-weights models cannot perform IICLL, limiting claims about 'LLMs' generally

Overclaimed 'perceptual grounding': LLMs lack embodied perception equivalent to humans; Gemini's image processing is qualitatively different from human sensorimotor grounding and this distinction should be clearly stated

Insufficient mechanistic understanding: Paper does not explain why efficiency bias emerges—is it inherent to language modeling, specific training procedures, or architectural choices? Speculation about input modality is underdeveloped
Incomplete robustness reporting: Claims that results were 'replicated with added input noise' but provides no results, methods, or analysis of these critical robustness checks
Underspecified IICLL implementation: Missing key details on number of color-pseudoword pairs per generation, number of generations, pseudoword generation procedure, and exact prompts used

Undefined 'counterfactual baseline': Figure 1H references a 'strong counterfactual baseline' but text never defines what these hypothetical variants are or how they were computed, limiting interpretability of key results

Limited analysis of model differences: Why does Llama consistently produce lower complexity? Why does Gemini-txt outperform Gemini-img on efficiency but not human-alignment? These patterns deserve systematic investigation

Insufficient human comparison: IICLL comparison relies on single human study [22]; more discussion of human variability and whether LLM patterns truly replicate human patterns would strengthen central claims

Training data contamination concern: While IICLL uses random initializations, cannot fully rule out that convergence patterns reflect memorized linguistic associations rather than genuine inductive biases

Unclear IB computation: How are mental representations operationalized from LLM outputs? How are I(M;W) and I(W;U) computed? Is Gaussian noise model appropriate for systems without human-like perception?
Limited ablation studies: No systematic investigation of model size, architecture, or training procedure effects; only input modality variations explored
WCS dataset limitations not addressed: Non-industrialized society focus may introduce cultural/economic biases; impact on comparisons not discussed

strengths: Novel IICLL methodology that enables direct comparison with human iterated learning experiments
Comprehensive evaluation of 39 LLMs across 6 families with systematic variation in size and training approach
Well-motivated research question with appropriate domain choice (color naming provides rich human data)
Clear empirical findings showing instruction-tuned models achieve better English alignment and Gemini 2.0 develops human-like IB-efficient systems
Rigorous evaluation framework grounded in Information Bottleneck theory with multiple validation approaches (efficiency metrics, NID alignment, rotation analysis)
High-quality presentation with excellent visualizations and extensive appendices supporting reproducibility
Strong reproducibility provisions including model identification, example prompts, and code commitment
weaknesses: Severely limited scope: nearly 95% of results are about color naming; Shepard circles experiment is preliminary (qualitative only, single model tested, no rigorous evaluation), undermining claims about general principles

Critical mechanistic questions remain unanswered: Why do LLMs evolve toward IB efficiency? Is it training data properties, instruction-tuning, model scale, or general inductive biases? This gap substantially limits the contribution's significance
Results overwhelmingly dependent on Gemini 2.0; other state-of-the-art models (Gemma, Llama, Qwen) show much weaker performance; no analysis of what distinguishes Gemini 2.0
Model collapse to single-word systems in smaller models (Appendix L) is buried in appendix despite being central to understanding necessary capabilities; should be prominent in main text

IICLL experimental design choices inadequately justified: sliding window history (10 interactions) differs from human experiments without sensitivity analysis; 6× vocabulary sampling choice unexplored; constrained vocabulary differs from human experiments
Selection bias: only models performing well on English naming tested in main IICLL; weaker models relegated to appendix; limits understanding of which capabilities enable efficiency

Brittleness to input format: performance severely degrades with CIELAB coordinates (Appendix C); described as testing 'ideal conditions' but suggests results may not reflect robust semantic understanding
Limited statistical testing: most comparisons rely on visual inspection and confidence intervals; formal significance tests largely absent
Most models fail at English color naming; observation that some produce WCS-like rather than English-like systems not investigated; incomplete analysis of failure modes

Heavy dependence on in-context learning capacity for IICLL results; unclear whether findings reflect semantic efficiency preferences or in-context learning ability; limited ablation distinguishing these factors
